title: Exponential share-size lower bounds for perfect secret sharing

importance.reason: A central storage lower-bound conjecture for arbitrary information-theoretic access control; it concerns every sharing scheme, including nonlinear ones with unrestricted computation.

category_assignment.reason: A fundamental limit on information-theoretic security or generic cryptanalysis, rather than a construction from an assumed primitive.

notes: Uses the one-bit, maximum share-alphabet length formulation of the exponential lower-bound conjecture; does not impose explicit access structures or efficient reconstruction.
The year records the dated primary problem source, not an assertion that the conjecture originated in 2019.
Distinct from active TCS-0465: its upper bound and this lower bound may both hold.

import_provenance.purpose: User-requested major cryptography problems outside primitive-construction implications. New candidates are red.

formal:
An access structure specifies which groups of participants may recover a secret; a perfect scheme gives exact recovery to those groups and no information to all other groups. Precise definitions appear in Model & notation. Is the following proposition true?
\[
\exists c>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \exists\Gamma_n\subseteq 2^{[n]}:
\quad\forall\text{ perfect schemes for }\Gamma_n,\qquad
\max_{i\in[n]}\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\ge 2^{cn}.
\]
Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the secret is one uniform bit, \(\Gamma_n\) is a monotone access structure with \(\varnothing\notin\Gamma_n\) and \([n]\in\Gamma_n\), and \(\mathcal S_i\) is participant \(i\)'s finite share alphabet. Here \(n_0\) is an integer, and the constants are universal. Sharing and reconstruction may be nonlinear and computationally unbounded.
definitions:
A monotone access structure \(\Gamma\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is a collection of authorized subsets such that \(A\in\Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq[n]\) imply \(B\in\Gamma\).

A perfect scheme is a joint probability distribution of a uniform secret \(B\in\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_i\in\mathcal S_i\), where every \(\mathcal S_i\) is finite and nonempty. For each authorized \(A\), a deterministic map from \(\prod_{i\in A}\mathcal S_i\) to \(\{0,1\}\) recovers \(B\) with probability one. For every unauthorized \(A\), the distributions of \((X_i)_{i\in A}\) conditioned on \(B=0\) and on \(B=1\) are identical. Arbitrary joint distributions are allowed; there is no field or linearity restriction.

The cost of a share is \(\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\) bits, and the scheme's cost is the largest of these costs. This measures alphabet size, not Shannon entropy. Rounding to an integer encoding length does not change the exponential-existence question. The access structures need not be efficiently recognizable, and the schemes need not be uniformly constructible. The statement concerns all sufficiently large integer participant counts, with one positive constant \(c\) chosen first.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified exponential lower bound, or a complete proof of its logical negation. A lower bound restricted to linear schemes or to bounded-complexity reconstruction does not meet the universal scheme quantifier. A merely superpolynomial lower bound does not establish the stated exponential bound.
why: This asks whether some access-control policies inherently require exponentially large pieces of a one-bit secret, even with unlimited computation. It would distinguish an intrinsic information cost from limitations of the constructions currently available.

context_blocks.text: For a threshold policy, any sufficiently large group can recover a secret and smaller groups learn nothing. General policies can specify much less regular combinations of participants. The conjecture asks whether that freedom forces an exponential storage cost in the worst case.

Larsen and Simkin study the exponential lower-bound conjecture attributed to Beimel. Their theorem forces either large shares or a large description of reconstruction; it does not remove the reconstruction restriction needed for an unconditional share-size lower bound.

Recent linear and multilinear lower bounds concern schemes whose algebraic structure restricts the sharing or reconstruction maps. Such restrictions are absent here. The September 2026 multislices paper proves exponential lower bounds for a broad family covering known general constructions, rather than for all perfect schemes.

The upper-bound question TCS-0465 asks whether every policy admits shares with an exponent below one half. This lower-bound question asks whether some positive exponential exponent is unavoidable. Both propositions can hold simultaneously; they express different sides of the storage gap.

progress.text: Larsen and Simkin prove an exponential obstruction when reconstruction descriptions are also constrained.
Beimel describes the exponential gap between general upper bounds and known general share-size lower bounds.
Beimel and Nir extend exponential lower bounds to a family covering currently known general constructions; the family restriction remains essential to their statement.

status_note: Targeted source and subsequent-work check on 6 November 2026 found no resolution for unrestricted perfect schemes. The 2026 results checked have explicit algebraic or construction-family restrictions. This is a bounded literature review, not an independent verification of their proofs.

sentences: Secret sharing distributes a secret so that prescribed groups can reconstruct it and all other groups learn nothing.
The question asks whether some policy at every sufficiently large participant count forces a positive exponential number of bits in at least one share.
The secret is one bit, and all finite, perfectly private schemes are allowed.
Known exponential lower bounds for restricted schemes do not settle this unrestricted question.
A resolution would identify a basic storage limit of information-theoretic access control.
